findings.message: "users"."name" is dropped and re-added in the same migration. Every existing value in this column will be lost.
findings.why: TypeORM drops and re-adds a column when its type or length changes, instead of changing it in place. The new column starts empty.
findings.safeAlternative: Change the type in place: ALTER TABLE "users" ALTER COLUMN "name" TYPE varchar(255). Widening a varchar, or changing varchar to text, does not rewrite the table. For other type changes, add a new column, backfill it, switch the code, and drop the old column in a later release.

findings.message: "users"."name" is added as NOT NULL without a default. The migration fails as soon as "users" has any rows.
findings.why: PostgreSQL fills a new column with its default for every existing row. With no default that value is NULL, which the NOT NULL constraint rejects.
findings.safeAlternative: Add the column as nullable, backfill it in batches, then enforce NOT NULL without a long lock (see no-set-not-null). Or add it with a constant default, which PostgreSQL 11 and later add without rewriting the table.

findings.message: "users"."bio" is dropped, which deletes every value in it.
findings.why: Dropping a column deletes its data immediately. Application code that still reads or writes the column fails until every running instance has the new version.
findings.safeAlternative: Remove the property from the entity and deploy that first. Drop the column in a later release, then suppress this finding with a reason.

suppressed.reason: bio removed from the entity in 2.3, deployed everywhere

findings.message: "users"."bio" is dropped and "users"."nickname" is added in the same migration. If this is a rename, every value in "bio" is lost.
findings.why: A renamed property can turn into a migration that drops the old column and adds a new one. The data is not copied, and no statement in the migration copies it. The dropped column type is not known here, so check whether the columns match.
findings.safeAlternative: Rename through expand and contract: add the new column, backfill it from the old one, switch the code, and drop the old column in a later release.
